02
Why I Built This

Living through the sudden surge of AI as a college student taught me something no syllabus did: adapting to new technology isn't optional anymore — it's the baseline for being ready to work.

What began as a personal effort to use these tools well turned into a bigger question when my professor and I started asking what AI would really mean for the job market my classmates and I were about to enter.

So instead of guessing, we decided to Measure — and then act on what we found. That instinct became a mission: to build a bridge between the classroom and the future of business. I help run initiatives that put students face-to-face with industry innovators, enterprise experts, and hands-on AI bootcamps — turning anxiety about the future into tangible career readiness, and helping a generation of students find their footing, and their voice, in an AI-driven world.

Learning In Real Time

AI didn't arrive on textbooks, assignments, references, or feedback. Working out how to study, build, and think alongside it became its own kind of education by the students themselves — one every student is now navigating at the same time.

Turning The Question Outward

What began as an individual challenge soon became a collective one. When an entire generation must adapt in real time, the most productive response is not anxiety but rigor — measuring what is actually happening and building resources students can genuinely use.

The Study, In Plain Terms

Before a campus AI & career-readiness bootcamp launched, our team needed to know where students actually stood. So we built a baseline study to measure three things — how career-ready students felt, how fluent they were with AI tools, and how much they believed in their own ability to succeed. Think of it as audience research before a campaign: you can't measure what moved the needle if you never captured the starting line.

The Paper
Abstract · the short version
AI Literacy and Career Readiness Confidence Among Undergraduates at a Public Urban University

Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping the labor market, yet undergraduates at public urban universities — particularly first-generation students — often arrive with limited AI exposure and underdeveloped career-readiness skills. This study reports baseline findings from a pre-bootcamp survey of 115 Brooklyn College (CUNY) undergraduates, measuring three domains: career-readiness confidence, AI literacy, and academic self-efficacy. Scores were moderate across all three (Career Readiness M = 3.14; AI Literacy M = 3.65; Self-Efficacy M = 3.50). Job-application preparedness was lowest (2.91) and prior AI use highest (3.79). AI literacy correlated significantly with career readiness (r = .26, p = .005), and career readiness correlated strongly with self-efficacy (r = .75, p < .001). No significant gaps appeared between first-generation and continuing-generation students, or between employed and unemployed students. Open-ended responses pointed to hopes of using AI for résumé writing, interview prep, and task efficiency — establishing an empirical baseline for evaluating AI-bootcamp programming for underrepresented students.

Keywords: AI literacy · career readiness · undergraduate students · first-generation college students · workforce development · higher education · bootcamp · CUNY

Full Research Paper

AI Literacy and Career Readiness Confidence Among

Undergraduates at a Public Urban University: Baseline Findings

from a Pre-Bootcamp Survey

Ngoc Cindy Pham, Jason Lin, Ruhshona Sayfiddinova

Brooklyn College, City University of New York

Koppelman School of Business

Author Note

Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Ngoc Cindy Pham, Koppelman School of Business, Brooklyn College, CUNY, 2900 Bedford Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11210. Email: <dr.ngocphamcindy@gmail.com>

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly reshaping the labor market, yet undergraduate students at public urban universities—particularly those who are first-generation college students—often enter higher education with limited exposure to AI and underdeveloped career readiness skills. This study presents baseline findings from a pre-bootcamp survey administered to 115 undergraduates at Brooklyn College, a mid-range public institution within the City University of New York (CUNY) system, prior to their participation in an AI and career readiness bootcamp series. Using a 15-item instrument, we assessed three domains: career readiness confidence, AI literacy, and academic self-efficacy. Descriptive analyses revealed moderate mean scores across all subscales (Career Readiness: M = 3.14, SD = 0.74; AI Literacy: M = 3.65, SD = 1.02; Self-Efficacy: M = 3.50, SD = 0.83). Notably, job application preparedness (Q7) returned the lowest item mean (M = 2.91), while prior AI tool use (Q8) was the highest (M = 3.79). A significant positive correlation was observed between AI literacy and career readiness (r = .26, p = .005), and a strong correlation between career readiness and self-efficacy (r = .75, p < .001). Independent samples t-tests indicated no significant differences between first-generation and continuing-generation students, nor between employed and unemployed students, across any subscale. Qualitative responses highlighted student aspirations to leverage AI for résumé writing, interview preparation, and task efficiency. These baseline findings establish an empirical foundation for evaluating the impact of AI bootcamp programming on underrepresented student populations in workforce preparation.

Keywords: AI literacy, career readiness, undergraduate students, first-generation college students, workforce development, higher education, bootcamp, CUNY

Introduction

The accelerating integration of artificial intelligence (AI) across professional sectors has generated a parallel urgency in higher education: how do institutions prepare undergraduate students to enter a labor market where AI fluency is increasingly expected? This question is especially pressing at public urban universities, which serve disproportionately high proportions of first-generation college students, students from low-income backgrounds, and students from historically underserved communities—populations that face compounding disadvantages in workforce readiness (Pearson et al., 2022; Kim & Sax, 2011).

Brooklyn College, a four-year liberal arts institution within the City University of New York (CUNY) system, exemplifies this context. With a majority-minority student body and a substantial percentage of first-generation students, Brooklyn College occupies an important but underexamined position in discussions about equitable access to emerging technology education. While elite universities have rapidly integrated AI curricula into their programs, mid-range public institutions have fewer resources and less established infrastructure for such programming (Meng et al., 2023).

In response to this gap, a series of AI and career readiness bootcamp sessions was developed and implemented for undergraduates at Brooklyn College. The bootcamp was designed to provide hands-on exposure to AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, résumé-writing assistants, job search automation), paired with structured career readiness activities including mock interviews, résumé workshops, and employer engagement panels. Prior to launching this program, a 15-item baseline survey was administered to assess students' pre-intervention levels of career readiness confidence, AI literacy, and self-efficacy.

The present paper reports on the pre-bootcamp survey findings. While the post-bootcamp follow-up survey is currently being collected, these baseline data offer valuable standalone insights into the needs, concerns, and aspirations of undergraduates at a mid-range public institution entering an AI-integrated professional landscape. Furthermore, they establish the empirical baseline against which intervention effects will be measured in future comparative analyses.

This study is guided by the following research questions:

RQ1: What are the baseline levels of career readiness confidence, AI literacy, and academic self-efficacy among undergraduates at Brooklyn College prior to an AI bootcamp?

RQ2: Do first-generation college students and non-first-generation students differ significantly in career readiness confidence, AI literacy, or self-efficacy?

RQ3: What relationships exist among career readiness confidence, AI literacy, and academic self-efficacy at baseline?

RQ4: What specific career-related hopes do students hold regarding the use of AI?

This study is grounded in Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT; Lent et al., 1994), which posits that career development is shaped by self-efficacy beliefs, outcome expectations, and personal goals. SCCT provides the theoretical scaffolding for the three core constructs examined here: students’ career readiness confidence maps onto domain-specific self-efficacy; AI literacy reflects outcome expectations regarding technology-mediated career tasks; and aspiration to use AI in one’s career represents goal-directed career behavior. This framework predicts that strengthening self-efficacy through structured, mastery-oriented experiences such as an AI bootcamp should produce cascading improvements in career readiness and goal commitment (Lent et al., 1994).

Literature Review

AI Literacy in Higher Education

AI literacy has emerged as a critical competency framework in educational and workforce discourse (Long & Magerko, 2020). Defined broadly as the ability to understand, evaluate, and use AI tools critically and responsibly, AI literacy encompasses multiple dimensions including technical knowledge, ethical awareness, and practical application skills (Ng et al., 2021). Despite growing calls for AI literacy integration into undergraduate curricula, empirical evidence on students' baseline AI knowledge remains sparse, particularly for students at under-resourced public institutions.

Prior studies suggest that AI literacy is unevenly distributed along demographic lines. Students with prior exposure to computer science coursework, male-identified students, and students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds tend to report higher AI familiarity (Lee & Kwon, 2024; Ng et al., 2021). These disparities raise equity concerns that are particularly salient in urban public university contexts where student populations may lack prior exposure but stand to gain substantially from AI skills development.

Career Readiness and Workforce Preparation

Career readiness—defined as the attainment of competencies required for post-collegiate employment successhas received sustained attention from researchers and practitioners (NACE, 2022). The National Association of Colleges and Employers identifies eight core career readiness competencies including career and self-development, communication, critical thinking, professionalism, and technology use. Among undergraduate students, self-reported career readiness tends to be lower among first-generation students and students with fewer internship or professional development opportunities (Kim & Sax, 2011; Stephens et al., 2015).

The intersection of AI and career readiness represents a new and rapidly growing area of inquiry. Researchers have begun to document how AI toolswhen properly integrated into career servicescan support résumé optimization, interview preparation, and job search efficiency (Yim & Su, 2024). However, students must first possess sufficient AI literacy to leverage these tools effectively, creating a dual competency demand that universities are only beginning to address.

First-Generation College Students and Educational Equity

First-generation college students (those whose parents did not complete a four-year degree) represent a substantial proportion of enrollment at public urban institutions (Pearson et al., 2022). This population faces distinctive challenges including limited social capital, reduced access to professional networks, and lower rates of participation in high-impact practices such as internships and research experiences (Stephens et al., 2015; Terenzini et al., 1996). These structural disadvantages may compound students' sense of career unpreparedness, making tailored programming particularly impactful for this group.

Bootcamp-Style Interventions in Higher Education

Short-format, intensive learning experiences—often termed bootcamps—have proliferated in both formal and informal educational settings as mechanisms for rapid skill acquisition (Thayer & Ko, 2017). Within higher education, bootcamp programming has been employed for coding instruction, entrepreneurship training, and professional development. Evidence on their effectiveness is mixed but generally positive when programs are well-structured, include experiential components, and provide follow-up support (Smith et al., 2017). The application of bootcamp models specifically for AI literacy and career readiness in undergraduate populations remains understudied.

Methods

Study Design and Setting

This study employed a cross-sectional survey design using pre-intervention data collected as part of a broader pre-post evaluation of an AI and career readiness bootcamp series. Data were collected at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, a four-year public liberal arts institution serving approximately 17,000 students in Brooklyn, New York. The institution enrolls a diverse student body, with a majority of students identifying as students of color and a significant proportion identifying as first-generation college students.

Participants

A total of 115 undergraduate students completed the pre-bootcamp survey (N = 115). Participants were recruited via course announcements and flyers distributed in undergraduate classes and student centers during the Spring 2026 semester. All respondents were enrolled undergraduates who voluntarily agreed to participate in the bootcamp series. Demographic characteristics are presented in Table 1.

Instrumentation

The pre-bootcamp survey consisted of 15 items: two demographic items (first-generation status; current employment), twelve Likert-scale items (1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree), and one open-ended item. Items were adapted from established career development and AI literacy frameworks (NACE, 2022; Ng et al., 2021; Long & Magerko, 2020) and piloted with a small group of students for clarity and relevance prior to administration.

Survey items were organized into three conceptual subscales: (a) Career Readiness (Items 3–7; five items assessing career clarity, résumé confidence, interview confidence, employer understanding, and job application preparedness), (b) AI Literacy (Items 8–10; three items assessing prior AI use, knowledge of AI for career tasks, and comfort with AI tools), and (c) Academic Self-Efficacy (Items 11–13; three items assessing communication confidence, help-seeking, and job market confidence). A final open-ended item asked: "What is one thing you hope AI can help you with in your future career?"

Internal consistency reliability was assessed for all three subscales using Cronbach’s alpha. Reliability was acceptable for the Career Readiness subscale (α = .78), the AI Literacy subscale (α = .81), and the Academic Self-Efficacy subscale (α = .76), indicating adequate internal consistency for research purposes (Nunnally, 1978).

Procedure

The survey was administered electronically via Google Forms at the beginning of the first bootcamp session, before any instructional content was delivered. Completion took approximately 8–12 minutes. Participation was voluntary, and students were informed that their responses would be used for program evaluation and research purposes. No identifying information was collected.

Data Analysis

Quantitative data were analyzed using Python (pandas, scipy.stats). Descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, frequency distributions) were computed for all items and subscale composites. Independent samples t-tests were used to compare subscale scores by first-generation status (first-generation vs. non-first-generation, excluding "prefer not to say" respondents) and employment status. Pearson correlations were computed to examine relationships among subscale composites. An alpha level of .05 was adopted for all inferential tests.

Open-ended responses (n = 107) were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Two researchers independently coded responses into emergent thematic categories. Prior to consensus discussion, inter-rater agreement was calculated at 84%, indicating acceptable reliability (Cohen’s κ = .79). Discrepancies were resolved through discussion until consensus was reached.

Results

Descriptive Statistics

Table 2 presents means and standard deviations for all survey items and subscale composites. Across the full sample, career readiness scores reflected moderate confidence, with the composite subscale mean of M = 3.14 (SD = 0.74). Item-level analysis revealed that job application preparedness (Q7: M = 2.91, SD = 0.98) was the lowest-rated item in the survey, while résumé confidence (Q4: M = 3.36, SD = 0.88) and career clarity (Q3: M = 3.33, SD = 0.89) were comparatively higher. Interview confidence (Q5: M = 3.22, SD = 0.89) and employer understanding (Q6: M = 3.08, SD = 0.92) fell between these extremes.

AI literacy scores yielded a composite mean of M = 3.65 (SD = 1.02), the highest of the three subscales. Prior AI tool use (Q8: M = 3.79, SD = 1.25) was the highest-rated item in the survey, indicating that most students had engaged with AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) prior to the bootcamp. Knowledge of AI for career tasks (Q9: M = 3.70, SD = 1.10) was similarly elevated, though comfort with AI for academic or career tasks (Q10: M = 3.44, SD = 1.16) was somewhat lower, suggesting partial translational knowledge gaps.

Self-efficacy scores yielded a composite mean of M = 3.50 (SD = 0.83). Help-seeking behavior (Q12: M = 3.68, SD = 1.01) and communication confidence (Q11: M = 3.60) were rated higher than job market competitiveness confidence (Q13: M = 3.22, SD = 0.98).

Group Comparisons

Table 3 presents results of independent samples t-tests comparing subscale scores by first-generation status and employment status. No statistically significant differences were found between first-generation students (n = 69) and non-first-generation students (n = 37) on any of the three subscales: AI Literacy (t = -0.93, p = .354, d = 0.18), Career Readiness (t = -0.38, p = .707, d = 0.07), or Self-Efficacy (t = 0.22, p = .826, d = 0.04). Effect sizes were uniformly small, consistent with the non-significant p-values. While non-first-generation students scored slightly higher on AI Literacy (M = 3.81 vs. M = 3.61), this difference was not statistically significant.

Similarly, no significant differences emerged between currently employed students (n = 65) and non-employed students (n = 50) on AI Literacy (t = 0.24, p = .810, d = 0.05). Employment was associated with marginally higher Career Readiness (M = 3.24 vs. M = 3.01, t = 1.69, p = .094, d = 0.32) and Self-Efficacy scores (M = 3.61 vs. M = 3.35, t = 1.66, p = .099, d = 0.31), with both approaching but not reaching conventional significance thresholds. These trends suggest that practical work experience may have a modest positive relationship with career confidence and self-efficacy that warrants investigation with larger samples.

Correlational Analyses

Table 4 presents Pearson correlations among the three subscale composites. AI Literacy was significantly and positively correlated with Career Readiness (r = .26, p = .005), suggesting that students with greater familiarity and comfort with AI tools also reported greater career preparedness. The correlation between AI Literacy and Self-Efficacy was positive but did not reach statistical significance (r = .15, p = .104). The strongest and most significant correlation was observed between Career Readiness and Self-Efficacy (r = .75, p < .001), indicating a robust relationship between students' confidence in their career skills and their broader academic self-efficacy.

Qualitative Findings: Aspirations for AI in Career

Open-ended responses were received from 107 of 115 participants (93% response rate). Thematic analysis identified four primary themes representing how students hoped to use AI in their future careers.

The most prevalent theme was Productivity and Efficiency, encompassing responses that emphasized AI as a tool for automating repetitive tasks, saving time, and managing information. Representative responses included hopes for AI to "help me complete tasks quicker," "alleviate tedious tasks," and "help with organizing data and information in a more professional manner."

The second most common theme was Career Preparation Support, reflecting desires to use AI for résumé writing, interview practice, and job search. Students expressed aspirations such as "polish my resume and build skills that I can share during interviews" and "I hope AI can help me perfect my resume and find job opportunities in my field."

A third theme, Skill and Knowledge Development, captured responses oriented toward learning and professional growth. Students wanted AI to help them "develop more critical hard skills," "learn new things," and "improve communication skills."

A fourth, smaller theme, Uncertainty and Ambivalence, encompassed responses from students who expressed skepticism or uncertainty: "I'm not sure I don't tend to trust AI" and "I hope AI would help me be more competitive on internships... (if that is ever possible)." This theme reflects the complex affective landscape students bring to AI engagement, suggesting that AI bootcamp programming must address not only skill gaps but also attitudinal barriers.

Discussion

This study presents pre-intervention baseline findings from 115 undergraduates at a public urban university prior to an AI and career readiness bootcamp. The results offer several important insights into the current state of AI literacy and career confidence among this population.

First, despite the widespread uptake of consumer AI tools like ChatGPT—reflected in the high mean for prior AI use (Q8: M = 3.79)students' comfort applying AI specifically to career tasks and their actual job application preparedness remained comparatively lower. This gap between general AI familiarity and applied career-oriented AI literacy mirrors findings from the broader AI literacy literature, which distinguishes between passive exposure and active, purposive use of AI tools (Ng et al., 2021; Long & Magerko, 2020). The bootcamp design specifically targets this translational gap by connecting AI tool use to concrete career tasks.

Second, the strong correlation between career readiness and self-efficacy (r = .75) aligns with Waldrop et al.’s (2024) work on academic self-efficacy in higher education, which posits that individuals’ belief in their own capabilities is closely intertwined with domain-specific performance expectations. This finding suggests that interventions targeting career readiness may simultaneously benefit students' broader self-efficacyand vice versa. Program designers working at the intersection of career services and AI education may find it productive to emphasize mastery experiences and positive reinforcement as mechanisms for building both constructs.

Third, the absence of significant differences between first-generation and non-first-generation students across all three subscales is noteworthy. While prior research has consistently documented disadvantages for first-generation students in career readiness outcomes (Kim & Sax, 2011; Stephens et al., 2015), our sample did not replicate these differences. This may reflect the particular characteristics of Brooklyn College's institutional context, where a high proportion of students are first-generation, potentially reducing the social capital differentials typically observed at more selective institutions. Alternatively, the sampling procedure—recruiting students who voluntarily enrolled in a career bootcampmay have introduced selection effects favoring more career-motivated students regardless of generational status. The null differences should be interpreted cautiously and revisited when post-bootcamp data are available.

Fourth, the rich qualitative data illuminate the texture of student aspirations and anxieties that quantitative measures alone cannot capture. The emergence of an Uncertainty and Ambivalence theme is particularly instructive for educators. Students who approach AI with skepticism may be less likely to fully engage with bootcamp activities unless programming explicitly addresses trust-building and ethical dimensions of AI use. This finding aligns with calls in the AI education literature for approaches that foreground critical AI literacy alongside technical skill development (Lee & Kwon, 2024).

Limitations

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional, single-institution design limits generalizability. Second, the self-report nature of the data introduces potential for social desirability bias, particularly on items assessing AI familiarity that students may perceive as evaluative. Third, the convenience sample of students who opted into a career bootcamp is likely more career-motivated than the general undergraduate population, potentially inflating scores on career readiness and self-efficacy. Fourth, the instrument, though adapted from established frameworks, has not been formally validated with published psychometric properties in this population. Finally, without post-bootcamp data, no causal inferences about intervention effectiveness can yet be made.

Implications and Future Directions

Notwithstanding these limitations, this study makes several contributions. It provides one of the first empirically grounded profiles of AI literacy and career readiness among undergraduates at a public urban institution, filling a gap in a literature dominated by studies from elite or private institutions. It also provides a methodological template for pre-post bootcamp evaluation that other institutions may adapt.

When post-bootcamp data are collected, planned analyses will include paired-samples t-tests and repeated-measures ANOVA to assess pre-post changes in subscale scores, as well as moderation analyses to examine whether intervention effects differ by first-generation status, employment status, or baseline AI literacy. Qualitative follow-up interviews with a subset of participants will also deepen understanding of the mechanisms through which bootcamp participation may influence career confidence and AI literacy.

Practitioners and administrators at public urban universities may draw several actionable insights from these baseline findings. The relatively low job application preparedness scores suggest this is a high-priority area for career programming. The high AI tool familiarity paired with lower applied confidence suggests that students need structured guided practice in applying AI tools to career tasks rather than introductory exposure. And the themes of uncertainty and ambivalence in qualitative responses signal the importance of building trust-centered, critically reflective AI pedagogy into bootcamp design.

Conclusion

As AI transforms the labor market, higher education institutions face growing pressure to ensure that all students—regardless of institutional selectivity, socioeconomic background, or generational status—develop the competencies required to thrive in an AI-integrated workforce. This paper reports baseline findings from a pre-bootcamp survey of 115 undergraduates at Brooklyn College, CUNY, revealing moderate career readiness and self-efficacy, moderately high AI familiarity with lower applied AI confidence, and rich student aspirations for AI-enabled career support. The strong relationship between career readiness and self-efficacy, and the significant correlation between AI literacy and career readiness, suggest that integrated programming addressing both domains simultaneously may yield mutually reinforcing benefits. Future work will evaluate whether the AI and career readiness bootcamp produces measurable pre-post gains and whether those gains are equitably distributed across student subgroups. These findings establish a rigorous empirical baseline for that evaluation while offering immediate insights into the needs and perspectives of undergraduates navigating the emergence of AI in professional life.
